title: Lumache al Sugo
subtitle: Lumache with slow-cooked pork and tomato ragù
excerpt: Lumache al sugo is pasta with a slow-cooked pork and tomato ragù: a weekend sauce that takes two hours to develop its depth. The lumache (snail shells) are a southern Italian pasta shape with a deep cavity that catches the sauce. It is a simple, deeply satisfying pasta that improves considerably if made a day ahead.
sourceNotes: Pasta al sugo di maiale (pork ragù) is a tradition across southern Italy, particularly in Campania and Basilicata. The long-simmered pork tomato sauce is the Sunday-lunch sugo eaten across much of the Italian south.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the ragù without the pasta for up to 3 months. Defrost in the fridge overnight and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: The ragù makes a generous batch: serve with pasta twice, or use the leftover sauce for bruschetta or polenta.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The ragù is better the next day. Make it fully, refrigerate overnight, and reheat before tossing with freshly cooked pasta.

glossaryTerms.definition: An Italian meat sauce simmered slowly until the meat breaks down and merges with the tomato base. Distinct from bolognese, which uses minced meat; a ragù often uses whole cuts that are shredded or autumn apart after long cooking.

content.text: Lumache al sugo is a two-hour sauce: pork ribs or shoulder braised slowly in tomatoes until the meat falls away from the bone and the fat from the pork enriches the tomato base. The lumache shape: named for a snail shell: has a deep cup that fills with the sauce. This is a Sunday dish in the Italian south, started in the morning and eaten at lunch.

items.prepNote: or pork shoulder, cut into large pieces

content.text: Brown the pork and build the
Heat the olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Season the pork and brown well on all sides, in batches, about 3 to 4 minutes per side. Set the pork aside.
Reduce the heat to medium. Cook the onion in the same pot for 6 to 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute. Add the red wine and let it evaporate, about 2 minutes.

Return the pork to the pot. Add the crushed tomatoes and basil stalks. Stir to combine. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook over the lowest heat for 2 to 2.5 hours, stirring every 30 minutes, until the pork is very tender and the sauce has thickened.
Remove the pork pieces and shred the meat from any bones. Return the shredded meat to the sauce. Add the basil leaves and season well.

Cook the lumache in well-salted boiling water until 1 minute short of al dente. Reserve a cup of pasta water, then drain. Toss with the ragù over medium heat, adding pasta water to loosen. Serve with a generous amount of grated pecorino.

items.symptom: Sauce is still thin and watery after 2 hours
items.cause: Heat was too low or lid was on throughout
items.fix: Remove the lid for the final 30 minutes of cooking to allow evaporation. If still thin, simmer uncovered, stirring frequently, until the sauce coats a spoon.

items.symptom: Pork is still tough after 2 hours
items.cause: The heat was too low or the pieces were too large
items.fix: Cut the pork into smaller pieces next time. Add a splash more liquid and cook for another 30 minutes. Pork ribs with bone cook faster than large boneless shoulder pieces.

items.cause: Tinned tomatoes were high-acid and the sauce needed longer to mellow
items.fix: Cook for longer: the extended simmering is what turns a sharp tomato sauce into a deep, rounded ragù. A small pinch of sugar can help at the seasoning stage.

content.text: The Sunday pork ragù is one of the most deeply embedded traditions of southern Italian home cooking. In Campania and Basilicata, the sugo di maiale: made with ribs, sausages, or shoulder: simmers on the hob from early morning, filling the house with the smell of tomatoes and pork fat. The pork is eaten as the second course; the sauce goes on pasta first. It is a structure that predates the modern idea of a single main dish and reflects the Italian tradition of using one long cook to produce two courses.
